account.intro: You are the first person on this instance, and the one who runs it.
account.title: Your account
account.username_hint: Lowercase, no spaces. It can't be changed: it's the name people will know you by here and on other instances.
code.error_expired: The code is no longer valid: the instance restarted and printed a new one. Look at the console again and type it in — I've kept everything else.
code.error_invalid: This code is not valid. It's the one printed in the instance's console, and it changes at every restart.
code.have_backup: Already have a backup to restore?
code.label: Code
code.title: The setup code
code.where: You'll find it printed in the instance's console when it starts. It never goes into the logs, and a new one is printed at every restart.
data.anonymous: This instance's data is on an anonymous volume. Docker created it on its own because nobody asked for one, and keeps it only when it is docker compose that recreates the container. If you update from the NAS panel, the instance starts empty every time: accounts, content, photos and the private key, which cannot be replaced.
data.ephemeral: This instance's data is inside the container. It disappears at the first image update — all of it, including the private key that makes the instance recognisable to its members, which cannot be replaced.
data.existed_body: Then the old data is almost certainly still on the machine: the volume that held it was not deleted, it has just been left with nobody using it. From a terminal on the machine, this lists the volumes that contain an ESTIA database, with the date it was last written:
data.existed_next: You'll get one for each time the instance started again from scratch. The most recent is the last setup you were using; you put it back by copying it into the folder you'll mount above, and the installation guide explains it step by step. Don't delete anything until you've checked that the instance is back with your things in it.
data.from_panel: From the NAS panel: stop the container, open it for editing, and in the volumes (or folders) section add a row that maps a folder of yours — for example /volume1/docker/estia/data — to the path /data inside the container. Then restart it.
data.from_terminal: From a terminal: use the docker-compose.yml file from the installation guide, which declares a named volume. It's also how updates stop asking you anything.
data.just_trying: If you're just taking a look at ESTIA and will throw it all away in ten minutes, start the container with ESTIA_ALLOW_EPHEMERAL_DATA=true and this screen will let you through.
data.refusal: I won't let you set it up like this. There's nothing inside yet, so fixing it now takes five minutes; later it would cost everything this community will have put into it.
data.title: First, let's give the data a home

recovery.confirm: I've written it down somewhere safe
recovery.intro: It's your instance's recovery code. It gets you back in if you forget your password, and this is the only time it is shown: the instance keeps only a fingerprint of it, and can't show it to you again.
recovery.title: Write this code down, now
recovery.where: Copy it onto a sheet of paper, into a password manager, onto a USB stick — wherever you like, as long as it isn't only on this computer. If you lose the code and the password, nobody can recover the instance.
restore.replace: Replace /volume1/docker/estia-backup with the folder where your backups are, {{archive}} with the file name, and /volume1/docker/estia/data with the data folder.
restore.step.dont_finish: Don't complete this setup form: that way you won't create a new instance with a key different from your backup's.
restore.step.restart: 5. Restart the container (or switch it on from the NAS panel) with the data folder mounted on /data. This screen will disappear and the instance will start again with all its content and accounts in place.
restore.step.run: Run the restore command and enter your private key (the one that starts with AGE-SECRET-KEY-1…) when asked:
restore.step.stop: Stop the web container (or make sure the destination data folder is empty and has no temporary estia.db in it).
restore.step.terminal: Open a terminal on the machine (or connect to the NAS over SSH).
restore.title: Restoring a backup
restore.why: Backups are encrypted, and the private key never goes through the browser. To protect the community's data even if the machine is stolen or compromised, the instance keeps only the public key it needs to write backups. Only you have the private key: it must never be typed into the browser or travel over HTTP (ADR 0013 and ADR 0016).
